newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian power demand spawns natgas growth.
newsitem.headline: Colombian power demand spawns natgas growth.

text.p: Colombian gas demand for electricity production is set to quadruple over the next 14 years, according to Texaco Colombia head Robert Galbraith.

At an energy conference here, he said natural gas accounted for 14 percent of the country's electricity generation in 1996 and saw this rising to over 30 percent by 2010, when total generation is expected to be twice its current level.
Galbraith saw Colombia's residential market as another major source of growth, taking up to 12 percent of the country's gas production in 2010, from five percent now.
"We see Colombia having a great future in natural gas and what we see is a lot of opportunities for investors in this field," he told conference delegates.

The whole sector has undergone a major restructuring over the last few years, and large capital investments have provided a network of pipelines extending across the northern and central parts of the country.
A blackout in the early 1990's hastened the expansion plan, when a severe drought hit hydro-electric electricity generation, which still accounts for 75 percent of the country's power.

Many of the hydro-electric plants have now been privatised, and the government is seeking investors to buy more generation assets and build gas-fired power stations to feed a projected doubling in electricity demand by 2010.
There is already a regulator established to oversee the reformed gas market and the government is this year farming out several distribution concessions.
Current gas production of 450 million cubic feet per day (mcfpd) is expected to grow to 800 mcfpd by 2000, according to government projections.
Galbraith said Colombian gas reserves were 11.5-18 trillion cubic feet, enough to last the country well over 50 years, and the gas was clean and cheap to extract.

Colombian wellhead prices were less than half those in the United States and less than a third of Canadian prices, he said. And he saw significant potential for growth in reserves from the little-explored offshore areas in the Pacific and the Caribbean.
